newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Confusion and scepticism as Mobutu returns home.
newsitem.headline: Confusion and scepticism as Mobutu returns home.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko, exhausted from fresh cancer treatment and a long flight from France, slipped quietly back into Zaire on Friday for what looked like one last attempt to cling onto power.

But the return of the man who has controlled the destiny of the sprawling Central African nation for over three decades caused confusion and scepticism, with critics and even some officials saying it would make little difference.

As if to underline the point more than 10,000 jubilant residents of Zaire's third city of Kisangani hailed Laurent Kabila and his rebels as saviours, when Kabila paid his first visit to the city on Friday.

"He is sure to come with his usual confusion. Everything is possible, a good move, a bad move and the worst possible move. But he will above all be thinking of himself," one highly placed member of the government told Reuters before Mobutu arrived.
In the event, there was confusion from the moment his plane landed when aides and his presidential guard ushered away a welcoming committee of senior military men and ministers.
"I think he was tired and did not want to be seen being helped down the aircraft steps," one government said later.
One aide to Mobutu, who has just had fresh cancer treatment in Europe, said the veteran president's wife had helped him down the steps.

The low-key return contrasted with Mobutu's December 17 homecoming when large crowds turned out to welcome him. This time, small crowds gathered in opposition areas on the airport route to jeer Mobutu and sing Kabila's praises.

Mobutu, 66, seized power as army chief in 1965. He has spent most of his time in Europe since having prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland in August. He left Monaco hospital on Wednesday after fresh cancer treatment.

The rebels, who hold major towns and territory in one fifth of Zaire, are advancing into the mining provinces of Kasai and Shaba -- the key to Zaire's economy. They have targeted the capitals of diamond-rich Kasai and copper-rich Shaba, Mbuji-Mayi and Lubumbashi, which is also Zaire's second city.
"If the rebels take Lubumbashi and Mbuji-Mayi it is finished, they will have taken the economy away from Kinshasa," one government member said.

Kinshasa street opinion is largely behind Etienne Tshisekedi, veteran leader of the radical Union for Democracy and Social Progress. Tshisekedi, a veteran Mobutu foe, enjoys huge popularity in the city's poorer quarters.
"Tshi Tshi is the man of the moment. He has the confidence of the population and if he gets together with Kabila it will be okay," says Fefe, 20, a security guard.
Tshisekedi's party has demanded that Mobutu endorse its leader as head of a new government to negotiate with Kabila.
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo has rejected an opposition-sponored vote in the transitional parliament to sack his government as invalid.

Tshisekedi has the backing of several leading allies of Mobutu, including Bemba Saolona, a millionaire businessman and one time financial advisor to the president but behind the scenes rival politicians are anxiously jockeying for position.
Elsewhere, support for Kabila, among a population hungry for change after three decades of hardship under Mobutu, is growing.
"Mobutu is at the heart of crisis, he is the problem. The solution now is Kabila. Mobutu is dying, and his return will change nothing," said Leonnie Lusamba, a waitress.
